name: Old City (Medina)
summary: The walled historic town on the harbour: Ottoman and Karamanli mosques, souqs, the Red Castle at its eastern corner, and the old Jewish quarters.
history: The street plan is ancient (Roman Oea), but the walls, mosques and souqs mostly date from the Ottoman and Karamanli periods (16th–19th centuries). Landmarks include the Arch of Marcus Aurelius (2nd century AD), the Dragut (Darghut) Mosque near the Bab al-Bahr sea gate (16th century), the Ahmed Pasha Karamanli Mosque (1730s) and the Gurgi Mosque (1830s). The Jewish community lived mainly in two quarters, the Hara Kabira and Hara Saghira, until anti-Jewish riots in 1945, 1948 and 1967 drove almost all of them out of Libya.
era: After 1969 the regime confiscated property left by Jews and Italians. As Tripoli spread outwards, many families left the Old City for newer districts, and its houses were increasingly let to poorer families and, later, migrant workers. Buildings decayed through the 1970s and 1980s. The Red Castle at the Old City’s edge was turned into the national museum. Gaddafi spoke to crowds from the Red Castle ramparts above Green Square on major occasions, including his speech of 25 February 2011.
today: Partly restored but still run-down in places; the souqs remain busy, and in recent years currency dealers have taken over parts of the old markets.
uncertain: Which Old City buildings the security services used in 1969–2011 is not documented in the archive. The OpenStreetMap point “The Turkish Prison” marks the Ottoman-era prison inside the walls.

sources.t: Wikipedia: History of the Jews in Libya
Al Jazeera (Arabic), 11 Feb 2020: Old City souqs turned into currency markets

name: City centre (Italian-era downtown)
summary: The grid of arcaded streets the Italians built south and east of the Old City after 1911, around today’s Martyrs’ Square (Green Square under Gaddafi).
history: Italian Tripoli was built between 1911 and the 1940s: Piazza Italia (later Independence Square, then Green Square, now Martyrs’ Square), the arcaded avenues, the Galleria De Bono, the Catholic cathedral (1923–28) on what became Algeria Square, a theatre and a railway station.
era: After the 1969 coup the square was renamed Green Square and became the regime’s stage for rallies, parades and speeches. In 1970 the cathedral was turned into the Gamal Abdel Nasser Mosque, the year Libya expelled its remaining Italian community and seized their property. Some Italian-era buildings were later demolished, including the Royal Miramare Theatre beside the Red Castle and the central railway station. In February 2011 protesters who tried to gather in Green Square were fired on.
today: Still the commercial heart of the city; the square has been called Martyrs’ Square since August 2011.
uncertain: Dates for individual demolitions under Gaddafi are not in the archive yet.

name: Dahra
summary: Older inner district east of the city centre, between the coast road and Ben Ashour, built up mostly in the Italian period.
era: Dahra lies between the government quarter of the city centre and the embassy district of Ben Ashour; several foreign embassies and Libyan state offices stood in or near it during the Gaddafi era.
today: A dense mixed residential and commercial area close to the centre.
uncertain: The archive does not yet tie specific security offices or arrests to Dahra. Family knowledge of the area would help.

name: Ben Ashour
summary: A well-off residential district south-east of the centre, with villas, embassies and ambassadors’ residences.
era: Under Gaddafi many embassies and diplomats’ homes were here. During the US air raid of 15 April 1986, bombs aimed at Bab al-Aziziya fell instead on homes in this area; houses were destroyed, civilians were killed, and the French embassy nearby was damaged. Libyan officials took foreign journalists to the damaged streets the next morning.
today: Still one of Tripoli’s more affluent districts, with many embassies and offices.
uncertain: Exact streets hit in 1986 and the number of civilian dead in Ben Ashour specifically are not settled in the sources.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1986 United States bombing of Libya

name: Fashloum
summary: A dense, older working-class neighbourhood east of the centre, south of Zawiyat al-Dahmani.
era: Fashloum was one of the first Tripoli neighbourhoods to rise against Gaddafi in February 2011; security forces fired on protesters and raided homes there in the days after 20 February 2011.
today: A crowded residential neighbourhood of narrow streets.
uncertain: Its role in earlier opposition, before 2011, is not documented in the archive.

name: Zawiyat al-Dahmani
summary: A coastal district east of the centre, between the sea and Fashloum; formerly the village of Shar al-Shatt.
history: The village of Shar al-Shatt was the scene of the battle and killings of 23–26 October 1911 at the start of the Italian invasion: Ottoman and Libyan fighters overran Italian positions, and Italian troops then killed hundreds of local civilians in reprisal.
era: Part of the inner city under Gaddafi; the 1911 battle was commemorated by the regime as a symbol of resistance to Italy.
today: Residential and commercial; reported under opposition control early in the August 2011 battle for Tripoli.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Battle and massacre at Shar al-Shatt

name: Al-Hani
summary: Eastern inner district between Fashloum and Souq al-Juma; site of the 1911 Battle of Hani (part of the Shar al-Shatt fighting), marked by a memorial.
history: Fighting around al-Hani in late October 1911 was part of the Ottoman–Libyan counter-attack on the Italian lines around Tripoli (the Shar al-Shatt battle). A monument to the Battle of al-Hani stands in the district today.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Battle and massacre at Shar al-Shatt

name: Bab Ben Ghashir
summary: Inner southern district between the city centre and Abu Salim.
uncertain: The archive has no documents tied specifically to this neighbourhood yet.

name: Sidi al-Masri
summary: Inner south-eastern neighbourhood around the Sidi al-Masri shrine and road, between Ben Ashour and Hadba.

name: Ras Hassan
summary: Small inner neighbourhood south of Ben Ashour.

name: Zanata
summary: Eastern neighbourhood between Hadba and Souq al-Juma.

name: Abu Sitta
summary: Coastal area east of the port with the Abu Sitta naval base and an old horse-racing course.
era: The naval base was one of the Libyan navy’s Tripoli facilities under Gaddafi.
today: In March 2016 the UN-backed Presidential Council arrived in Tripoli by sea and set up at the Abu Sitta naval base.

name: Gurji
summary: West-central residential district along the Gurji road, between the centre and Hay al-Andalus.

name: Al-Mansoura
summary: Small inner-west neighbourhood next to Gurji and Bab Akara.

name: Bab Akara
summary: Inner neighbourhood south-west of the centre, close to the northern side of Bab al-Aziziya.

name: Bab al-Aziziya (neighbourhood)
summary: The streets named after the Bab al-Aziziya gate, next to the former Gaddafi compound of the same name.
era: Living beside Gaddafi’s headquarters meant checkpoints, closed roads and a heavy security presence; the area was hit in the 1986 US raid and again by NATO in 2011.

name: Hay Dimashq
summary: Residential neighbourhood between Abu Salim and Hadba.

name: Tekbali camp
summary: Army camp in the Salah al-Din area of southern Tripoli, named after the late Khalifa al-Takbali. On 12 May 2025 the militia leader Abdel Ghani al-Kikli was killed at a meeting here, setting off days of fighting across the city.
era: The camp lies in the belt of army bases south of Salah al-Din that the Gaddafi regime built up around the capital. Its current name, honouring “the late Khalifa al-Takbali”, appears in sources only after 2011, so it was probably known by another name or a number before then.
today: On 1 July 2013 the Third Support Brigade, which had guarded the camp since Gaddafi’s forces were driven from Tripoli, handed it to the national army at a ceremony attended by the head of the General National Congress and the interior minister. By 2025 it was associated with the 444th Brigade: al-Kikli, head of the Stability Support Apparatus, was killed at a meeting at Tekbali camp on 12 May 2025, and his escorts and 444th Brigade guards exchanged fire outside.
uncertain: The camp’s name and units under Gaddafi, and who Khalifa al-Takbali was.

sources.t: LANA (Libyan state news agency), 1 Jul 2013: army takes over the “late Khalifa al-Takbali” camp

name: Yarmouk camp (32nd Brigade)
summary: Large army base south of Salah al-Din, home of the 32nd Reinforced Brigade — the “Khamis Brigade”, commanded by Gaddafi’s son Khamis.
era: The Khamis Brigade was the regime’s best-armed unit and its main defence of Tripoli in 2011. As the city fell in late August 2011, the bodies of dozens of detainees were found in a burned warehouse near the brigade’s base — the Yarmuk massacre.
today: In the 2019–2020 war Haftar’s forces used Yarmouk as a command centre for the southern Tripoli front; government forces said they retook it on 23 May 2020.

sources.t: Al Jazeera, 23 May 2020: GNA retakes Yarmouk, Sawarikh and Hamza camps

name: Artillery and Missile School
summary: Army artillery and missile training school south of Tripoli, next to the Yarmouk camp; locally “the missiles camp” (al-Sawarikh).
today: Government forces said they retook al-Sawarikh camp from Haftar’s forces on 23 May 2020.
uncertain: Whether the OpenStreetMap “Artillery and Missile School” is the same site news reports call al-Sawarikh camp.

sources.t: Al Jazeera, 23 May 2020: GNA retakes Yarmouk, Sawarikh and Hamza camps

name: Hamza camp
summary: Army camp in southern Tripoli, west of the Yarmouk camp.
today: Government forces said they retook Hamza camp from Haftar’s forces on 23 May 2020.

sources.t: Al Jazeera, 23 May 2020: GNA retakes Yarmouk, Sawarikh and Hamza camps

name: Transport camp
summary: Military transport camp on the southern edge of the city, on the way to the old international airport.

name: 7 April camp
summary: Military camp in south-western Tripoli. Its name recalls 7 April — the date of the 1976 student crackdown and of the public hangings held on that anniversary — a typical Gaddafi-era name.
uncertain: What units used the camp before 2011.

name: Camp 27
summary: Military base west of Janzour, named after kilometre 27 on the coast road west of Tripoli.
today: Fought over repeatedly after 2011, including clashes between the 52nd and 55th brigades for control of the camp.

sources.t: Libya Security Monitor: clashes between 52nd and 55th brigades over Camp 27

name: Military College, al-Hadba
summary: Military college in the al-Hadba area of southern Tripoli.
today: On 4 January 2020 an air strike hit cadets gathered on the parade ground, killing about 30 young men aged 18 to 22. The Tripoli government blamed Haftar’s forces, which denied it.

name: Central Security headquarters
aliases: General Administration of Central Security at the Ministry of Interior
الادارة العامة للامن المركزي بوزارة الداخلية
summary: Headquarters of the Interior Ministry’s Central Security force, in the Salah al-Din area.

name: Ghut al-Shaal mobilisation camp
summary: “Tajyeesh” (mobilisation) camp in Ghut al-Shaal. Under Gaddafi, military training was compulsory for secondary-school and university students, and mobilisation centres like this one ran it.
uncertain: Exact dates and use of this camp.

name: Abu Sitta naval base
summary: Navy base on the coast east of the port.
today: The UN-backed Presidential Council landed here by boat on 30 March 2016 and used the base as its first seat in Tripoli.

name: Tajura naval base
summary: Navy base on the coast east of Tajura.

name: Libyan Naval Academy, Janzour (Sidi Bilal)
summary: The navy’s academy on the Janzour coast, by the Sidi Bilal port.
era: On 15 April 1986 US aircraft bombed the Sidi Bilal port facility, which the US said trained naval commandos.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1986 United States bombing of Libya

name: Air-defence missile site
summary: A surface-to-air missile site south-east of the city. Under Gaddafi, Tripoli was ringed by Soviet-supplied air-defence missile batteries.
era: During the US raid of 15 April 1986 Libyan air defences around Tripoli fired heavily; in 2011 NATO struck Libyan air-defence sites in the first days of its campaign.
uncertain: Whether this particular site dates from the Gaddafi era.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1986 United States bombing of Libya

name: 42nd Brigade headquarters
summary: Headquarters of a post-2011 army brigade in the Ain Zara area.

name: 55th Brigade
summary: Base of the 55th Brigade, a post-2011 unit, next to Camp 27 west of Janzour.

name: Al-Ma‘asra
summary: An area marked as military near Gurji in today’s map data; the name means “the press” (as in an olive press).
uncertain: Its history and use are not documented in the archive.

name: Electronic support site
summary: A military area marked “electronic support” south-west of the city.
uncertain: Its history and use are not documented in the archive.

name: Military camp, Tajura
summary: Military camp on the eastern side of Tajura.

name: Mitiga airport (former Wheelus Air Base)
summary: Airport in Souq al-Juma: the Italian Mellaha air base, then the US Wheelus Air Base (1943–1970), then the Libyan Okba Ben Nafi air base; later also used as a civil airport.
era: The US handed Wheelus over on 11 June 1970; it became the Libyan air force’s Okba Ben Nafi base.
today: Tripoli’s only working airport since 2014. The Rada force controls it and runs a prison there; an ICC suspect faces charges over abuses at Mitiga prison in 2014–2020.

name: Tajoura Nuclear Research Centre
aliases: Renewable Energies and Water Desalination Research Centre
summary: Libya’s main nuclear research site, east of Tajura, built with Soviet help around a 10-megawatt research reactor.
era: The reactor began operating in the early 1980s. The centre was part of the nuclear programme Libya renounced in December 2003.
uncertain: The map point is approximate.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Libya and weapons of mass destruction

name: Red Castle (Assaraya al-Hamra)
summary: The fortress at the corner of the Old City overlooking Martyrs’ (Green) Square, seat of Tripoli’s rulers for centuries and now a museum.
era: Under Gaddafi it housed the national (Jamahiriya) museum. Gaddafi addressed crowds from its ramparts, most famously on 25 February 2011.

name: The Turkish Prison (Old City)
summary: The Ottoman-era prison inside the Old City walls, labelled “The Turkish Prison” in today’s map data.
uncertain: Whether it held prisoners after 1969.

name: Ain Zara prison (“the political prison”)
summary: Prison in Ain Zara that OpenStreetMap labels “the political prison”. The map treats its use for political detainees before 1989 as suspected.
today: Hundreds of inmates escaped during clashes in September 2018.

name: Al-Mabani detention centre
summary: Migrant detention centre in Ghut al-Shaal, opened in 2021 and criticised by the UN and rights groups for overcrowding and abuse.

name: Tripoli Zoo
summary: The city zoo and park in Abu Salim, next to the Bab al-Aziziya compound.
today: In May 2025 the missing-persons authority received reports of mass graves at the zoo, after the Abu Salim fighting.

name: Port of Tripoli
summary: Tripoli’s commercial harbour, north-east of the Old City.
today: Taken by the 444th Brigade in the May 2025 fighting.

name: Former women’s military academy
summary: Former academy of Gaddafi’s female bodyguards (the so-called “Amazons”), between the port and the city centre.
today: Most buildings were demolished around 2017; the site opened as a public park in 2021, keeping only the old gate’s control tower.
uncertain: The map point is approximate (“between the port and the city centre”).

name: Abu Salim
summary: A large, mostly working-class district south of the centre; home to Abu Salim prison, the city zoo and, on its northern edge, the Bab al-Aziziya compound.
era: Abu Salim prison, built inside a military police compound and completed in 1984, became the regime’s main prison for political detainees. On 29 June 1996 about 1,270 prisoners were killed there in what is known as the Abu Salim massacre; families were not told for years, and their protests over it in Benghazi helped spark the 2011 uprising. During the battle for Tripoli in August 2011 Abu Salim was one of the last districts held by Gaddafi loyalists.
today: After 2011 the district was dominated by the Stability Support Apparatus of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli (“Ghnewa”). After he was killed in May 2025 there was heavy fighting in Abu Salim, and the government said it had taken control. In May 2025 more than 50 unidentified bodies were reported in the Abu Salim hospital morgue and the missing-persons authority received reports of mass graves at the zoo.
uncertain: Where in the district the 1996 victims were buried has never been fully established.

name: Hadba al-Khadra
summary: Southern district (“the Green Plateau”) east of Abu Salim, with housing estates, hospitals, the University of Tripoli’s southern faculties and a military college.
era: Mostly built up during the Gaddafi years as the city grew south. The map marks Hadba al-Khadra prison as a suspected site; it is documented as a prison only after 2011.
today: After 2011 al-Hadba prison held senior Gaddafi-era officials, including the former intelligence chief Abdullah al-Senussi and Gaddafi’s son Saadi. On 4 January 2020 an air strike on the military college at al-Hadba killed about 30 cadets.
uncertain: Whether the al-Hadba prison buildings were used for detention before 2011 is not established.

sources.t: Al Jazeera, 5 Jan 2020: attack on military academy in al-Hadhba

name: Salah al-Din
summary: Southern district with large military camps: Tekbali camp, the Yarmouk camp (once the base of the Khamis Brigade) and other army facilities lie in and around it.
era: Under Gaddafi the area south of Salah al-Din held major army bases. The 32nd Reinforced Brigade, commanded by Gaddafi’s son Khamis and the best-equipped unit in the army, was based at the Yarmouk camp. In late August 2011, as Tripoli fell, the bodies of about 45–50 prisoners were found in a burned warehouse near the brigade’s base: the Yarmuk massacre.
today: The southern camps were front lines in the 2019–2020 war for Tripoli and in the May 2025 clashes, which began with the killing of Abdel Ghani al-Kikli at Tekbali camp.

name: Ain Zara
summary: Large south-eastern district of farms and newer housing; site of a 1911 battle and of a prison long known locally as the political prison.
history: On 4 December 1911 Italian forces attacked the Ottoman–Libyan positions at the Ain Zara oasis in one of the main battles around Tripoli; a memorial stands near the site.
era: Mostly farmland and scattered settlement in the 1970s and 1980s. OpenStreetMap labels the prison here “the political prison – Ain Zara”; the map treats its use for political detainees before 1989 as suspected but not confirmed.
today: Ain Zara prison was badly hit in the clashes of September 2018, when hundreds of inmates escaped. The district was a front line in the 2019–2020 war and was taken by the 444th Brigade in the May 2025 fighting.
uncertain: When the Ain Zara prison was built, and who was held there before 2011.

name: Al-Furnaj (University area)
summary: Eastern-central district around the main campus of the University of Tripoli (called Al-Fateh University under Gaddafi).
era: The university was a centre of student opposition. On 7 April 1976 students at the universities in Tripoli and Benghazi protested against military control and called for elections; the protests were met by violent counter-demonstrations and many students were imprisoned. On 7 April 1977 students were hanged in public in Benghazi, and public executions were held on the 7 April anniversary in following years until the late 1980s. The Washington Post reported on 23 April 1984 on hangings in Tripoli that drew attention to Libyan dissent.
today: Still the main university campus; renamed the University of Tripoli after 2011.
uncertain: Which executions took place on the Tripoli campus itself, and on which dates, still needs confirming against Amnesty International reports of the period.

sources.t: Washington Post, 23 Apr 1984: “Hangings in Tripoli Focus Attention on Libyan Dissent”
Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, “Libya: The significance of 7 April”, LBY40606.E, 7 Jan 2003 (cited by Wikipedia)

name: Souq al-Juma
summary: Large eastern district built over old oasis villages and farms; Mitiga airport (the former Wheelus Air Base) lies inside it.
era: Wheelus Air Base, the largest US air base outside the United States in the 1960s, was handed over on 11 June 1970 and renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base; the date became the “Evacuation Day” holiday. In February 2011 Souq al-Juma was one of the first districts to rise, and its residents played a leading part in the August 2011 uprising inside Tripoli.
today: Since 2011 the district has been dominated by the Rada (Special Deterrence) force, which runs Mitiga airport and a prison inside it.

name: Tajura
summary: Coastal town east of Tripoli with a 16th-century history, a Soviet-built nuclear research centre and naval and military sites.
history: In 1551 Ottoman forces based at Tajura took Tripoli from the Knights of St John; the Murad Agha Mosque dates from that era.
era: The Tajoura Nuclear Research Centre, with a Soviet-supplied 10-megawatt research reactor, began operating in the early 1980s and was part of Libya’s nuclear programme until it was given up in 2003.
today: On 2 July 2019 an air strike hit the Tajoura migrant detention centre, killing more than 50 people.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Libya and weapons of mass destruction

name: Janzour
summary: Coastal town on Tripoli’s western edge; the Sidi Bilal port and naval school, bombed in 1986, lie on its shore.
era: The US raid of 15 April 1986 struck the Sidi Bilal port facility, described by the US as a training site for naval commandos. The Libyan naval academy is also in Janzour.
today: A large residential suburb; it saw fighting between armed groups at several points after 2011.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1986 United States bombing of Libya

name: Gargaresh
summary: Western coastal district along Gargaresh Road, a long commercial strip of shops and restaurants.
era: Seaside villas and beaches in the Italian and monarchy periods; it grew into a busy suburb under Gaddafi.
today: Home to many migrant workers. On 1 October 2021 security forces raided the district and detained around 5,000 migrants.

name: Hay al-Andalus
summary: Affluent western district of villas and apartment blocks between Gurji and Gargaresh, with several embassies.
era: Largely developed from the 1970s onward as Tripoli expanded west along the coast.

name: Al-Siyahiya
summary: Western coastal district (the name means “the tourist area”) with beaches, hotels and several embassies.

name: Ghut al-Shaal
summary: Western district south of Gargaresh, with an army mobilisation (tajyeesh) camp and, since 2021, the al-Mabani migrant detention centre.
today: Al-Mabani detention centre opened in 2021 and has been criticised by UN agencies and rights groups for overcrowding and abuse.

name: Al-Dribi
summary: Western residential district of villas south of Hay al-Andalus.

name: World Islamic Call Society
summary: Headquarters and college of the World Islamic Call Society, founded under Gaddafi in 1972 to spread Islam abroad.
era: The society trained foreign students and funded mosques and schools across Africa and Asia; it was also a channel for Gaddafi’s foreign influence.

name: Qasr bin Ghashir
summary: Town south of Tripoli next to Tripoli International Airport.
era: The military side of Tripoli International Airport was one of the targets of the US raid of 15 April 1986; Libyan aircraft on the ground were destroyed.
today: Tripoli International Airport was wrecked in the fighting of July–August 2014 and has not reopened; the area was a front line again in 2019–2020.

sources.t: Wikipedia: 1986 United States bombing of Libya

name: Al-Karimia
summary: South-western outskirts of farms and newer housing on the road to Aziziya.

name: Sawani bin Adam
summary: Southern farming town on Tripoli’s outskirts.

name: Al-Hadba Project
summary: Southern area that grew out of a Gaddafi-era development “project” (mashrou), now largely residential.
uncertain: What kind of project it began as (agricultural or housing) and when.

name: Former shanty neighbourhood (Hay al-Akwakh)
summary: OpenStreetMap labels this area “formerly the huts neighbourhood” — one of the informal settlements on Tripoli’s edge.
uncertain: When the huts were cleared and where residents were moved. Family memory would help here.
